narrative.note: Right now every subject on Riley's report is just getting started, and each one comes with one clear, simple next step to build from this month.

subjects.math: Right now, counting five objects one at a time and saying how many there are is where the math picture starts, and that's a completely normal starting point at this age.
subjects.literacy: Asking what a sign or cereal box says out loud is the next literacy step for Riley, and it usually clicks once print starts feeling meaningful.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is the next phonics skill on deck for Riley.
subjects.writing: A fingers-first crayon grip is the next step for Riley's writing, and it usually follows a lot of hand strength building first.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier in the day is the next language step, the start of real storytelling for Riley.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, big versus small, animals versus plants, is the next science step for Riley.
subjects.social_studies: Naming how family members connect, like grandma being mommy's mom, is the next social studies step for Riley.
subjects.art: Naming the main colors while drawing or painting is the next art step for Riley.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is the next music step, right at the edge of where it typically shows up for Riley's age.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping, with one foot leading the other, is the next gross motor step for Riley.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is the next fine motor step, right at the edge of where it typically shows up for Riley's age.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing with other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is the next step, right at the edge of where it typically shows up for Riley's age.
subjects.self_care: Daytime toileting, with just the occasional miss, is the next self-care step for Riley.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, is the next step, right at the edge of where it typically shows up for Riley's age.
subjects.computer_science: Giving exact step-by-step instructions during play, and following yours, is a fun next step to try whenever you like.
subjects.spanish: Understanding common everyday words in another language, like water, milk, or more, is a fun next step whenever you like to lean into it.

drawers.math: This is the moment where number words start clicking into actual counting. Count the stairs makes it easy to add in: counting stairs, crackers, or toy cars, touching each one as they go.
drawers.literacy: The letter hunt turns any errand into practice: picking one letter and hunting it on cereal boxes, street signs, and book covers. Curiosity about words usually shows up before reading does.
drawers.phonics: Breaking a word into its beats is one of the earliest building blocks for reading later. Sound I-spy builds the ear for it in the car, the bath, or the grocery line.
drawers.writing: Grip strength comes before grip habit, so any squeezing, tearing, or pinching play helps first. Rainbow name turns name practice into art: writing it big, tracing it in two more colors, then decorating it.
drawers.language: This skill often shows up once there's enough vocabulary to hold a memory in order. Tell it back gives easy practice: after anything fun, they narrate what happened and you add the reactions.
drawers.science: Sorting is early classification, the seed of scientific thinking. Sink or float makes the guessing itself the science: gathering five small things and guessing before each goes in the bowl.
drawers.social_studies: Understanding how people connect to each other is a real cognitive leap at this age. Map of home makes it visual: drawing your house together and marking everyone's bed with a star.
drawers.art: Color words often take longer to arrive than color recognition itself, so this is common. Draw the song pairs naming with feeling: playing a song and drawing how it feels, fast scribbles for fast parts.
drawers.music: Steady beat is the foundation under rhythm and later reading fluency too. Copy my clap is an easy game: clap a short pattern, they echo it, then swap who leads.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping asks for a new kind of balance and coordination that takes real practice to click. Animal races makes it playful: racing down the hallway as a bear, a crab, then a frog.
drawers.fine_motor: Stringing beads takes real hand-eye coordination and patience together. Snipping strips builds the same hand control: cutting paper into strips and snipping confetti into a jar with safe scissors.
drawers.social_emotional: Turn-taking is a skill that grows with practice and a lot of reminders, not something that just appears. Name it to tame it helps in the moment: name the feeling first, then offer two choices.
drawers.self_care: This one comes together on its own schedule for every child, and readiness matters more than age. The button board turns practice into a game: buttoning a shirt around a cushion and racing the timer.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting is hard because it asks a young mind to hold still on purpose. Freeze dance dresses that up as fun: music on, dance big, music off, freeze.
drawers.computer_science: Giving precise step-by-step instructions is early programming logic in disguise. Robot parent makes it a giggly game: they program you across the room, wrong steps included, and you follow exactly.
drawers.spanish: Exposure at this age is about what the family does together, not about hitting a milestone. One phrase week keeps it simple: pick one useful phrase and use it all week at natural moments.
